original_question: Is it algorithmically decidable whether a given element g ∈ CT(Z) (a) permutes a nontrivial partition of Z into residue classes? (b) has only finite cycles? (c) has no finite cycles?
target_in_paper: Problem 21.74 in the New Problems section of the 21st issue (2026) of The Kourovka Notebook, with CT(Z) defined by the earlier Problem 17.57.
correct_elements: Your draft already identifies the exact target almost verbatim: it is an algorithmic decidability question for a given element g in CT(Z), and it preserves the paper’s three separate cases: (a) whether g permutes a nontrivial partition of Z into residue classes, (b) whether g has only finite cycles, and (c) whether g has no finite cycles.
missing_details: The draft is not stand-alone because it does not define the group CT(Z). In the paper, CT(Z) is the group generated by all class transpositions τ_{r1(m1),r2(m2)} of Z; this definition is given earlier in 17.57.
The notation r(m) should be unpacked: for integers 0 <= r < m, r(m) = {r + km | k in Z}.

A class transposition should be defined explicitly: for disjoint residue classes r1(m1) and r2(m2), τ_{r1(m1),r2(m2)} is the involution that interchanges r1 + km1 with r2 + km2 for each k in Z and fixes all other integers.
For an algorithmic question, the input must be effectively encoded. A stand-alone formulation should say that g is given effectively, for example as a finite word in class transpositions.
In part (a), 'nontrivial partition' should be made explicit, e.g. a partition with at least two parts, so that the trivial one-block partition {Z} is excluded.
In part (a), 'partition of Z into residue classes' should be made explicit as a partition whose parts are pairwise disjoint residue classes covering Z.
In parts (b) and (c), the meaning of 'cycles' should be spelled out as cycles in the permutation action of g on Z, equivalently orbits of the cyclic group <g> acting on Z.
Part (c) is ambiguous unless one states explicitly whether fixed points count as finite cycles; a stand-alone version should avoid this by saying that every orbit is infinite.
It is worth making explicit that (a), (b), and (c) are three separate decision problems, exactly as in the paper.
refined_question: Let r(m) = {r + km | k in Z} for integers 0 <= r < m, and for disjoint residue classes r1(m1), r2(m2) let τ_{r1(m1),r2(m2)} be the involution of Z that interchanges r1 + km1 and r2 + km2 for each k in Z and fixes all other integers. Let CT(Z) be the subgroup of Sym(Z) generated by all such class transpositions. Given an element g in CT(Z), effectively presented for example by a finite word in class transpositions, is there an algorithm deciding, separately, whether (a) g permutes some nontrivial partition of Z into residue classes, i.e. a partition Z = A1 ⊔ ... ⊔ Ak with k >= 2 in which each Ai is a residue class and g{A1,...,Ak} = {A1,...,Ak}; (b) every cycle of g on Z is finite; and (c) every cycle of g on Z is infinite?
justification: The nearest official formulation is exactly Problem 21.74; your draft is already essentially a transcription of it. The only substantive work needed is to inline the earlier definition of CT(Z) from 17.57 and to make the input model and the meanings of 'nontrivial partition', 'finite cycles', and 'no finite cycles' explicit so that the question is fully stand-alone. It should not be replaced by neighboring CT(Z) problems such as 21.73 (conjugacy in CT(Z)) or older subgroup-orbit questions, because 21.74 is the direct and precise match.
